title: My Daily Brief
overview: This edition is led by reports that the FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its National Crime Information Center, and by President Trump's comments on the hack in a Fox News interview. In the same interview he said he would work with Democrats on a credit card interest rate cap. Other stories include Mexico's capture of FBI most-wanted cartel figure 'Chapo Isidro', the signing of an EU-Indonesia trade deal, two Charlotte-area homicide arrests, a bus crash in Seoul, and BTS's sweep at the MAMA Awards.

stories.headline: FBI investigating apparent breach of national crime database
stories.summary: The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), according to media reports citing unnamed people familiar with the matter. CNN first reported the breach. The NCIC is a database that local, state and federal police use for warrants, missing persons, stolen property and background checks. The FBI has not publicly confirmed the incident or commented. It is unclear when or how the intrusion happened, or whether data was taken. President Trump told Fox News he had 'just heard about it' and that 'it's not good.' The report follows a September breach claimed by the ShinyHunters hacking group and a string of recent US tech outages, which officials have said were not cyberattacks.
key_facts: The FBI declined to comment or did not respond to outlets' requests for comment.
Trump on Fox News: 'We just heard about it and I will say that it's not good. I don't like that.'
In September, ShinyHunters claimed a breach tied to the FBI's job portal; the group claimed to have data on about 38,000 bureau staff.
Trump replaced National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross this week after a series of tech disruptions.
There is no indication so far that the NCIC incident is linked to ShinyHunters or to the recent outages.

perspectives.framing: PBS, running AP copy, kept to the basics: one anonymous source, the FBI declining comment, and earlier FBI hacks. Al Jazeera placed the breach within a string of government breaches and outages. It said Trump 'has repeatedly downplayed breaches,' highlighted his 'positive spin' and 'Russia hoax' remarks, and noted that FBI Director Kash Patel skipped a congressional threat hearing.

BleepingComputer, the BBC and The Hill focused on what the NCIC does and what remains unknown. They also cited the earlier ShinyHunters breach. The BBC added a former NSA analyst's comments and noted a separate reported cyberattack on the USDA farm payment system.

The Daily Caller, citing three sources via Fox News, described the database as one that 'tracks fugitives and monitors sex offenders.' It quoted Trump's full remarks, including the Russia hoax reference, and Patel's statements on the ShinyHunters arrests. It listed recent outages and noted the Cairncross replacement.

disputed: The FBI has not confirmed the breach; reports rely on anonymous sources, variously numbered as one (AP), two (CNN) or three (Fox News).
When the breach happened, how attackers got in, and whether any data was stolen are all unknown.
Outlets differ on whether Trump's remarks amount to confirmation: CNBC said he 'confirmed' it, while Al Jazeera said he 'appeared to confirm' it.
Whether the breach is connected to the recent nationwide outages is unknown.
stories.why: Police across the country rely on the NCIC daily, so a compromise could affect sensitive records and public safety.

stories.headline: Mexican forces capture FBI most-wanted cartel leader 'Chapo Isidro'; at least 11 killed
stories.summary: Mexican special forces arrested Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as 'Chapo Isidro' and listed among the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives, in Guasave, Sinaloa, late Friday. Mexico's defense ministry said the arresting force came under attack with gunfire and explosives. It said seven alleged gunmen and four soldiers were killed and eight people were arrested, including Meza Flores' alleged second-in-command and a financial operator. Mexican officials said US intelligence helped locate him but gave few details. Violence followed overnight, including roadblocks, burning vehicles and civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, before calm largely returned Saturday. Meza Flores was flown to Mexico City to face prosecution; the US had offered a $5 million reward and has charged him with drug trafficking.
key_facts: At least 11 people were killed: 7 alleged cartel gunmen and 4 Mexican soldiers.
Eight people were arrested; three were flown to Mexico City and five were handed to prosecutors in Sinaloa.
The US offered a reward of up to $5 million; Meza Flores was indicted in the US in 2012, with a superseding indictment in 2019.
A Mexican Pacific League baseball game in Guasave was abandoned as gunfire broke out.
US Ambassador Ronald Johnson credited 'sustained cooperation and trust.'

perspectives.framing: PBS (AP) and The Guardian emphasized the violence and civilian fear, quoting a local journalist. AP noted experts' warnings that removing cartel leaders can trigger new waves of violence. Both cited Trump's pressure on Mexico and the limited detail on US-Mexico coordination.

The BBC and DW covered both the operational details and the casualties. They noted Trump's pressure, including threats of military action, and the recent run of arrests of cartel figures. DW quoted the US ambassador and noted the uncertainty about extradition.

Fox News framed it as a 'joint U.S.-Mexico operation' and quoted the defense ministry's three-phase account at length, along with the FBI poster's charges. The Washington Examiner gave a brief report noting the US intelligence help. Neither of these articles discussed experts' warnings about follow-on violence.

disputed: The extent of US involvement: Mexico cited 'intelligence coordination' but gave few details, while Fox called it a joint operation.
Extradition: the BBC says the US is seeking it, while DW says it is unclear whether Mexico will extradite him.
Outlets describe his organization differently, as the Meza Flores organization (Guasave Cartel) or as leading the Beltrán Leyva group.
Online videos of helicopters firing on the city have not been independently verified.
stories.why: The arrest marks escalating US-pressured action against cartels and the violent fallout such operations can bring for civilians.

stories.headline: Trump says he would work with Democrats to cap credit card interest rates
stories.summary: In a Fox News interview Saturday, President Trump said he would work with the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress on his proposed one-year 10% cap on credit card interest rates. 'These credit card companies have made a lot,' he said. Trump first proposed the cap in January, but it stalled amid bank opposition and little Republican interest. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, expected to chair the Senate Banking Committee, and Republican Sen. Josh Hawley both welcomed the remarks. Banking groups have warned that a cap would restrict credit for less creditworthy borrowers.
key_facts: The median credit card rate is about 22.2% (New York Fed survey, August).
US credit card balances are a record $1.29 trillion, up 67% since early 2021, according to the New York Fed.
Warren: 'Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money.'
Researchers estimated that a 10% cap would save Americans about $100 billion a year in interest.
Democrats take control of Congress in January.

perspectives.framing: PBS (AP) stressed that Trump could not deliver the promise under a GOP Congress because of industry pressure and Republican indifference. It presented research suggesting large consumer savings while noting industry warnings.
Axios and The Hill framed it as possible bipartisan common ground. Axios set the consumer savings argument against the banking industry's warning that a cap would deny credit to millions.

Fox Business framed it as an opening for a bipartisan deal amid record consumer debt. It quoted Trump's defense of the cap against free-market objections and highlighted support from both Hawley and Warren, while noting bank opposition. The Washington Examiner published a brief report on the exchange.

disputed: Banks say a cap would cut access to credit and rewards; supporters cite research saying the industry would remain profitable.
Whether Congress will actually take up legislation, and in what form, is unclear.
stories.why: A cap would directly affect the borrowing costs of the roughly 195 million Americans with credit cards.

stories.headline: Opinion: Fox News column criticizes DOJ's backing of OpenAI in copyright case
stories.summary: A Fox News opinion piece argues that the Justice Department went too far by filing a statement of interest supporting OpenAI's 'fair use' defense in lawsuits brought by The New York Times and other news organizations. The lawsuits accuse OpenAI and Microsoft of using millions of articles to train AI without permission. The writer says the DOJ's position departs from more balanced White House and G20 guidance and would favor large AI firms. The column also argues that property rights require compensation for creators. This is an opinion column, not news reporting.
key_facts: News organizations including The New York Times are suing OpenAI and Microsoft over AI training on their articles.
The DOJ filed a statement of interest supporting OpenAI's fair use position.
The DOJ argues that licensing costs could hamper smaller firms, US AI leadership and national security.

perspectives.framing: The opinion column frames the DOJ brief as an 'extreme' interpretation of fair use that conflicts with the administration's own AI framework. It casts copyright as a property right and calls on large AI companies to pay creators.

disputed: Whether AI training qualifies as fair use is the central unresolved legal question before the courts.
The characterization of the DOJ position as 'extreme' is the columnist's view.
stories.why: The outcome could determine whether AI companies must pay for the content used to train their systems.

links.title: Americans don’t have to choose between our AI future and ripping off copyright owners

stories.headline: Two men arrested after fatal shooting at Monroe convenience store
stories.summary: Monroe, N.C., police arrested two men after a fatal shooting shortly before midnight Friday at Sammy's Mini Mart on East Sunset Drive. Police said a physical fight in the parking lot between Luis Zazocoteco, 22, and Jose Francisco Barcelo Suarez led to the shooting. Zazocoteco was charged with second-degree murder. A bystander, Khalil Hailey, 34, allegedly fired a gun into the air and was charged with possession of a firearm by a felon. The investigation is ongoing.
key_facts: Zazocoteco is charged with second-degree murder; an arrest warrant alleges he killed Suarez.
Surveillance video shows a fight followed by a single shot, according to WSOC.
Hailey, said to be a convicted felon, was not involved in the fight, police said.
Both men were held at the Union County Detention Center.

perspectives.framing: Local TV outlets reported the police account. WSOC added surveillance video and interviews with the store owner, who described both men as regular customers and blamed drinking.
The only left-leaning article in this group, from The Guardian, concerns an unrelated police shooting on Flinders Island, Tasmania, and does not cover the Monroe case.

disputed: Police did not publicly say who fired the fatal shot, though the warrant alleges Zazocoteco killed Suarez.
When Suarez died was not immediately clear.
stories.why: It is a local homicide case in Union County that is still under investigation.

stories.headline: Trump says FBI hack could have a 'positive spin'
stories.summary: Speaking to Fox News about the reported breach of the FBI's crime database, President Trump said it was 'not good' but suggested it might reveal information about what he called the 'Russia, Russia, Russia hoax' and voter fraud. 'I always like to put things on a positive spin,' he said. Sources told MS NOW that the database includes fingerprint records and data on wanted persons, violent felons and missing persons; it is restricted to law enforcement but not classified. The FBI did not comment.
key_facts: Trump: 'Maybe we'll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place.'
Trump: 'I wonder who's doing it, because wouldn't it be great to learn about Russia, Russia, Russia?'
The NCIC is restricted to law enforcement but not classified, according to CNBC's sources.

perspectives.framing: CNBC and The Hill focused on Trump's own words. Axios framed the remarks as showing his focus on past grievances with the FBI while public alarm grows about the vulnerability of government infrastructure.
The Washington Examiner reported that Trump said the hack might expose voter fraud and the 'Ukraine hoax.' It noted that he found the attack deeply concerning but chose a 'positive spin.'

disputed: Trump's claims of past voter fraud and his description of the Russia investigation as a 'hoax' are his assertions.
What data, if any, was taken in the breach is unknown.
stories.why: The president's response shapes how seriously the administration is seen to be treating a major security incident.

stories.headline: Suspect charged with murder in east Charlotte park death
stories.summary: Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police identified the man found dead with an apparent gunshot wound in east Charlotte on Wednesday as 21-year-old Daniel Velasquez Mejia. Franz Menchu Dominguez has been charged with first-degree murder, armed robbery and possession of a stolen firearm. Mejia's mother told WSOC her son had been missing since Friday, and his car was found at the scene.
key_facts: The victim, Daniel Velasquez Mejia, was 21.
Suspect Franz Menchu Dominguez faces charges of first-degree murder, armed robbery and possession of a stolen firearm.
Police found the body Wednesday, Nov. 18, while responding to an attempt-to-locate call.

perspectives.framing: Local outlets reported the police identification and charges, with WSOC adding comments from the victim's mother.

disputed: Outlets describe the location differently: Sheffield Park, the Evergreen Nature Preserve area, or 'woods.'
QCN says he was killed on Wednesday, while his mother said he had been missing since Friday.
stories.why: It is an arrest in a local homicide case.

stories.headline: EU and Indonesia sign trade deal removing most tariffs
stories.summary: The EU and Indonesia signed a comprehensive trade and investment agreement in Brussels on Saturday, almost a decade after talks began. The deal removes tariffs on more than 98% of EU exports to Indonesia. Indonesia says about 90% of its exports to the EU will be tariff-free, benefiting palm oil, footwear and textiles. It includes a dedicated palm oil protocol addressing deforestation concerns. The European Parliament must approve the deal and Indonesia must ratify it before it takes effect.
key_facts: The EU estimates savings of over €600 million a year in customs duties.
The EU projects GDP gains by 2042 of €16 billion for the EU and €27 billion for Indonesia.
Von der Leyen: 'one of the most ambitious deals the European Union has concluded in Asia.'
Indonesian President Prabowo is due to visit Brussels on Dec. 11.

perspectives.framing: CNA and DW presented the deal as part of EU efforts to diversify trade amid tensions with the US and China, relying on official statements from both sides. A BBC article grouped with this story covers a separate UK-EU deal: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said it will take effect regardless of a tuition fee dispute, while Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called it 'not fair.'

disputed: Timing of entry into force: CNA says early next year, DW says 2027.
The GDP and export projections are EU estimates.
stories.why: It shows the EU deepening trade ties in Asia as relations with the US and China grow harder.

stories.headline: Bus crash near Seoul's Hongik University Station injures six
stories.summary: A bus veered onto the pavement and hit a structure near Hongik University Station in Seoul on Saturday at about 6:57 p.m. It happened after a collision involving another bus and a sedan. Six people were taken to hospitals, with no deaths or serious injuries reported. Police and fire authorities are investigating the cause.
key_facts: Six people were injured; no deaths or serious injuries were reported.
The crash happened around 6:57 p.m. in a busy entertainment district.

perspectives.framing: Yonhap and The Korea Herald, which republished the Yonhap report, gave identical factual accounts.

disputed: The exact cause is under investigation.
stories.why: It was a traffic incident in one of Seoul's busiest nightlife areas.

stories.headline: BTS wins five awards at 2026 MAMA Awards in Osaka
stories.summary: BTS won five trophies at the two-day MAMA Awards at Kyocera Dome Osaka, including artist of the year and album of the year for 'Arirang.' The group was on its world tour and accepted its awards by prerecorded video. Cortis won song of the year for 'RedRed' a year after its rookie award, and Enhypen won fans' choice of the year for the second straight year. Big Bang won three awards, including music visionary of the year.
key_facts: BTS won 5 awards, including 2 of the 4 grand prizes.
Cortis won song of the year for 'RedRed.'
Enhypen won fans' choice of the year for a second consecutive year.
Alpha Drive One and Tuide shared best new artist.

perspectives.framing: The Korea Herald and Yonhap focused on BTS's comeback after a nearly four-year hiatus, Cortis's rise and acceptance speeches. Yonhap included a full winners list.

stories.why: The results reflect the K-pop industry's major acts and its rising groups.

investigations.question: What is happening with AI regulation in the US and EU?
investigations.update: No articles directly address US or EU AI regulation. Tangentially, a Fox News opinion column criticizes the DOJ for backing OpenAI's fair use defense in AI copyright lawsuits, and notes that the White House AI framework acknowledges arguments on both sides.
